pancreatic-cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic-cancer.definition: Pancreatic cancer is a cancer that starts in the pancreas, an organ that helps with digestion.
pancreatic-cancer.overview: Pancreatic cancer often causes no symptoms at first, and when symptoms appear they can be vague. The NHS says it can be difficult to treat. Smoking, long-term diabetes, chronic pancreatitis and some inherited conditions are linked to a higher risk, although having risk factors does not mean a person will get it. Treatment can include surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and when a cure is not possible the focus is on controlling symptoms.
causes: The exact cause of pancreatic cancer is not known
Risk factors such as smoking and long-term diabetes are linked to it, but having risk factors does not mean a person will get the cancer
riskFactors: Smoking
Long-term diabetes
Chronic pancreatitis
Inherited conditions and a family history of the disease
Being overweight or obese
Older age
signs: Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)
Weight loss without trying
Changes to bowel habits, such as diarrhoea or constipation
complications: A blocked bile duct, causing jaundice
Problems with digestion and nutrition
Spread of the cancer to other parts of the body
Pain, tiredness and nausea
pancreatic-cancer.diagnosis: The diagnosis, and the type of pancreatic cancer, is made by a biopsy, which is a sample of tissue from the pancreas. Imaging such as a CT scan is commonly used to assess the cancer. NICE recommends a pancreatic protocol CT scan for people with jaundice, before the bile duct is drained. If the diagnosis is still unclear, NICE says a PET-CT scan, an endoscopic ultrasound or both, with tissue sampling, may be offered.
pancreatic-cancer.treatment: The NHS says treatment depends on the size and type of the cancer, where it is, whether it has spread and the person's general health. Surgery is possible only when the cancer can be removed, and it can also relieve symptoms such as jaundice or blockages when it cannot. Chemotherapy can be given before or after surgery or to control the cancer, and the NHS says radiotherapy is not often used. Targeted therapy is another option listed by MedlinePlus. Supportive care helps with symptoms such as pain, tiredness, nausea and digestion problems.
pancreatic-cancer.prevention: Smoking is a risk factor that can be changed. Cancer Research UK says there is no national screening programme for pancreatic cancer in the UK, but people at high risk may be able to have tests, sometimes as part of a study.
pancreatic-cancer.seekCare: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for yellowing of the skin or eyes, or for vomiting that lasts more than 2 days. Pancreatic Cancer UK says jaundice needs a GP or A&E straight away. A GP appointment is advised for noticeable weight loss without trying, or for other symptoms that continue or get worse after 2 weeks. Having these symptoms does not definitely mean a person has pancreatic cancer.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of pancreatic cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says pancreatic cancer often causes no symptoms at first. Cancer Research UK says it does not usually cause symptoms in the early stages, and Pancreatic Cancer UK says symptoms may not be specific to the disease and can come and go at first.

Yellowing of the skin or eyes, called jaundice, is one of the common signs, and the NHS says it can come with itchy skin, darker urine and paler stools. The NHS also lists loss of appetite, losing weight without trying, tiredness and fever or chills. Digestive symptoms include feeling or being sick, diarrhoea or constipation, bloating and indigestion. The NHS describes pain in the upper abdomen and back that can ease when leaning forward. Cancer Research UK and Pancreatic Cancer UK list tummy or back pain among the signs, and Pancreatic Cancer UK also lists indigestion.

The NHS says these symptoms are common and often have other causes. Having them does not definitely mean a person has pancreatic cancer.

sections.heading: What causes pancreatic cancer, and who is at higher risk?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says the exact cause of pancreatic cancer is not known. The National Cancer Institute says some risk factors, such as smoking, can be changed, while others, such as genetics and family history, cannot. Having risk factors does not mean a person will get pancreatic cancer. Reviews describe cigarette smoking, long-term diabetes and obesity as established risk factors. Diabetes can be both a risk factor for pancreatic cancer and a result of it, and newly diagnosed diabetes can be an early sign. Chronic pancreatitis, long-term inflammation of the pancreas, is one of the strongest associations, although only a small proportion of people with it develop pancreatic cancer.

Some inherited conditions, including BRCA2 and Lynch syndrome gene changes, raise the risk, but most cases are not linked to a family history. MedlinePlus says the risk increases with age and that a family history slightly increases the chance. Cancer Research UK says there is no national screening programme for pancreatic cancer in the UK. People at high inherited risk may be able to have tests, sometimes through a study such as EUROPAC.

sections.heading: How is pancreatic cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says the diagnosis, and the type of pancreatic cancer, is made by a pancreatic biopsy, and that more tests then show how far the cancer has spread. Cancer Research UK says a CT scan is commonly used to assess pancreatic cancer, and a PET-CT scan may be used to find out more, for example whether it has spread outside the pancreas. A hospital NHS page describes an abdominal ultrasound and blood tests as usually the first step in finding the cause of jaundice.

NICE guidance recommends a pancreatic protocol CT scan for people with jaundice before the bile duct is drained. If the diagnosis is still unclear, NICE says a PET-CT scan, an endoscopic ultrasound or both, with tissue sampling, may be offered.

A biopsy can be taken during an endoscopic procedure such as ERCP or endoscopic ultrasound, or with a long, fine needle passed through the wall of the abdomen and guided by ultrasound or CT. ERCP is an endoscopic examination that lets doctors see the duct system and collect samples. Macmillan says a small tube called a stent is usually placed during an ERCP to hold a blocked bile duct open.

sections.heading: How is pancreatic cancer treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says pancreatic cancer is difficult to treat. The NHS says the choice depends on the size and type of the cancer, where it is, whether it has spread and the person's general health. Whether an operation is possible depends on whether the cancer can be removed, and removal may involve part, or rarely all, of the pancreas along with nearby organs. If the cancer cannot be removed, surgery may still be used to help control some symptoms, such as jaundice or blockages. MedlinePlus says some people whose cancer can be surgically removed are cured, but in most people the tumour has already spread and cannot be completely removed at diagnosis.

The NHS says chemotherapy can be given before surgery to shrink a tumour, after surgery to lower the risk of the cancer coming back, or to control the cancer when surgery is not an option. It says radiotherapy is not often used and, when it is, usually goes with chemotherapy or eases symptoms of advanced cancer. Cancer Research UK describes chemotherapy as the main treatment for stage 4 pancreatic cancer, where it might help people live longer and relieve symptoms. MedlinePlus also lists targeted therapy as an option.

sections.heading: Living with pancreatic cancer and managing symptoms
sections.body:
Cancer Research UK says advanced pancreatic cancer cannot normally be cured, but treatments can control symptoms and improve quality of life. Macmillan says it will not be possible to cure pancreatic cancer for many people. The National Cancer Institute says palliative therapy can improve quality of life by controlling the symptoms and complications of pancreatic cancer. Macmillan says a GP or cancer specialist can refer a person to a palliative care team, made up of doctors and nurses who work to keep symptoms under control.

The NHS says supportive care covers issues such as enzyme replacement tablets for digestion problems, pain relief and medicine for sickness. Macmillan says pain can be treated with radiotherapy, painkillers or nerve blocks, alone or together.

A tumour that blocks the bile duct stops bile draining, which causes jaundice, and the build-up of bile can cause itching. A stent, usually placed during an ERCP, holds the duct open so that bile can drain. If a stent is unsuccessful or not possible, surgery such as a bypass may be able to relieve the blockage. Specialist nurses or doctors may also suggest creams or medicines to ease the itch.

faqs.q: Can pancreatic cancer be cured?
faqs.a: Cancer Research UK says advanced pancreatic cancer cannot normally be cured, but treatment can control symptoms and improve quality of life. Macmillan says it will not be possible to cure pancreatic cancer for many people. MedlinePlus says some people whose cancer can be surgically removed are cured, but in most people the cancer has spread and cannot be completely removed at diagnosis.

faqs.q: Does pancreatic cancer always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says pancreatic cancer often causes no symptoms at first. Cancer Research UK says it does not usually cause symptoms in the early stages, and Pancreatic Cancer UK says symptoms can come and go at first. The NHS adds that the symptoms are common and often have other causes.

faqs.q: Is there a screening test for pancreatic cancer?
faqs.a: Cancer Research UK says there is no national screening programme for pancreatic cancer in the UK, but people at high risk may be able to have tests, sometimes as part of a study. Pancreatic Cancer UK offers an online family history checker for people concerned about inherited risk. MedlinePlus says a family history slightly increases the chance of developing the cancer.

faqs.q: When should someone see a doctor about possible symptoms?
faqs.a: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for yellowing of the skin or eyes, vomiting for more than 2 days, or diarrhoea for more than 7 days. It advises a GP appointment for noticeable weight loss without trying or for symptoms that continue or get worse after 2 weeks. Pancreatic Cancer UK says jaundice needs a GP or A&E straight away.

prostate-cancer.name: Prostate cancer
prostate-cancer.definition: Prostate cancer is a cancer that starts in the prostate, a small gland in the male reproductive system that sits just below the bladder.
prostate-cancer.overview: Prostate cancer often causes no symptoms at first. When symptoms appear they are usually changes to passing urine. The NHS says it often grows slowly and may never cause problems, so treatment is not always needed. Age, Black ethnicity and family history are linked with a higher risk. The NHS PSA test page says there is no national screening programme, and the UK National Screening Committee has recommended targeted screening for some men with a BRCA2 gene change.
causes: The causes of prostate cancer are largely unknown, according to NHS 111 Wales
Inherited changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes can raise the risk, according to Prostate Cancer UK
riskFactors: Increasing age
Being from a Black ethnic background
A father or brother who has had prostate cancer, with the risk greater if the relative was diagnosed at a younger age
A BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene change
A family history of breast or ovarian cancer
signs: A weak urine flow
Needing to pass urine urgently, often or during the night
Blood in the urine or semen
Unexplained weight loss in advanced disease
complications: Spread of the cancer beyond the prostate, which may need chemotherapy
Lower back pain and unexplained weight loss in advanced disease
Radiotherapy side effects such as urinary and bowel irritation and erection problems
Hormone therapy side effects such as hot flushes, tiredness and weight gain
prostate-cancer.diagnosis: The NHS 111 Wales page lists blood tests, a digital rectal examination, an MRI scan and a biopsy as the most commonly used tests for prostate cancer. If a person is referred to a specialist because prostate cancer is possible, the NHS says an MRI scan is arranged. A biopsy may follow, in which a small needle is put into the prostate to take a tissue sample to be checked for cancer cells. If cancer is found, the NHS lists a CT scan, MRI scan, PET scan and bone scan as further tests that help decide on treatment.
prostate-cancer.treatment: The NHS says treatment is not always necessary, and that for early cancer without symptoms it can be delayed until symptoms appear. When treatment is needed it may include surgery, radiotherapy and hormone therapy, with chemotherapy if the cancer has spread. Macmillan describes active surveillance as monitoring the cancer with regular PSA blood tests and MRI scans, with a biopsy usually only if there are signs the cancer may be growing. The NHS says hormone therapy on its own does not cure prostate cancer but can slow it down and help with symptoms.
prostate-cancer.prevention: The Surrey and Sussex Cancer Alliance says prostate cancer is not linked to any clear preventable causes. The NHS says there is currently no national screening programme for prostate cancer, and the UK National Screening Committee has recommended targeted screening only for some men with a BRCA2 gene change and a family history of cancer.
prostate-cancer.seekCare: The NHS lists seeing a GP as non-urgent advice if a person has trouble passing urine or other symptoms of prostate cancer, or is worried about their risk. Many of these symptoms have other causes, such as an enlarged prostate, so they do not by themselves mean a person has prostate cancer.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of prostate cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says prostate cancer often causes no symptoms at first. When symptoms do appear, they are usually changes to passing urine. The NHS lists difficulty starting to pass urine, a weak flow, needing to go urgently or often, and getting up to pass urine during the night. Erection problems and blood in the urine or semen are also listed.

In more advanced cases, the NHS lists lower back pain and unexplained weight loss. The NHS describes an enlarged prostate as a very common non-cancerous condition that becomes more likely as men get older and can cause similar urinary symptoms.

The NHS lists seeing a GP as non-urgent advice if a person has trouble passing urine or other symptoms of prostate cancer, or is worried about their risk of prostate cancer.

sections.heading: Who is at higher risk of prostate cancer?
sections.body:
Macmillan says prostate cancer is uncommon before the age of 50 and more common over the age of 75. Prostate Cancer UK says the condition mainly affects men over 50.

Macmillan says Black men have a much higher risk of prostate cancer and tend to develop it at a younger age.

Macmillan lists a father or brother who has had prostate cancer as a risk factor, with a greater risk if the relative was diagnosed at a younger age. Macmillan also lists a family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Prostate Cancer UK says changes in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes can raise the risk of prostate cancer but do not guarantee it, and that such changes are uncommon.

sections.heading: Is there a screening programme for prostate cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS PSA test page says there is currently no national screening programme for prostate cancer in the UK, because the PSA test is not always accurate. It says routine PSA testing is not currently offered on the NHS unless genetic tests have shown a faulty version of the BRCA2 gene.

The UK National Screening Committee has made a final recommendation for targeted screening. It recommends PSA testing every 2 years for men aged 45 to 61 who have a BRCA2 variant that can cause disease and a family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer. It did not recommend screening the whole population or men with a family history but no BRCA2 variant, and it says it is still uncertain whether screening would do more good than harm for Black men.

The NHS says a raised PSA level may be a sign of prostate cancer but can also be caused by another condition, such as an enlarged prostate, prostatitis or a urinary tract infection, so a high result does not mean a person has cancer.

sections.heading: How is prostate cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales lists blood tests, a digital rectal examination, an MRI scan and a biopsy as the most commonly used tests for prostate cancer. A digital rectal examination is a physical examination of the prostate, and the Royal Marsden says it cannot diagnose cancer on its own.

If a person is referred to a specialist because prostate cancer is possible, the NHS says an MRI scan is arranged, which gives a clearer view of the prostate and shows whether more tests are needed. If more information is needed, a biopsy may be suggested, in which a small needle is put into the prostate to take a tissue sample to be checked for cancer cells.

If cancer is found, the NHS lists a CT scan, MRI scan, PET scan and bone scan as further tests that help the team decide on treatment.

sections.heading: How is prostate cancer treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment is not always necessary, and that for early cancer without symptoms it can be delayed until symptoms appear. When treatment is needed it may include surgery, radiotherapy and hormone therapy, and chemotherapy may be needed if the cancer has spread.

Macmillan describes active surveillance as monitoring the cancer with regular tests instead of treating it straight away. It involves regular PSA blood tests and MRI scans, and a biopsy is usually only needed if there are signs the cancer may be growing. Macmillan says this avoids or delays the side effects of surgery or radiotherapy, and that treatment is offered if the cancer grows more quickly or symptoms develop.

The NHS says radiotherapy uses high-energy radiation to kill cancer cells. Brachytherapy is a form of internal radiotherapy in which radiation is placed in the prostate. The NHS says hormone therapy on its own does not cure prostate cancer but can slow it down and help with symptoms.

sections.heading: Side effects of treatment and support
sections.body:
Macmillan says radiotherapy for prostate cancer can cause urinary and bowel irritation and problems getting or keeping an erection. Cancer Research UK lists problems with erections, bowels or passing urine among the long-term effects of external radiotherapy. Macmillan says brachytherapy causes similar side effects, and that on its own it is less likely than external radiotherapy to cause late bowel effects, although short-term urinary effects may be more severe.

Hormone therapy has its own side effects. Macmillan lists tiredness, difficulty sleeping, hot flushes and weight gain, and St George's adds loss of sex drive, erection problems and breast swelling or tenderness. Prostate Cancer UK says hormone therapy can weaken the bones.

NHS 111 Wales advises that people with side effects from treatment should be referred to specialist services, such as continence services.

faqs.q: Does the NHS screen for prostate cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS PSA test page says there is currently no national screening programme for prostate cancer, and routine PSA testing is not offered unless genetic tests have shown a faulty BRCA2 gene. The UK National Screening Committee has recommended targeted screening for men aged 45 to 61 with a BRCA2 variant and a family history of certain cancers, and ministers in England have agreed to a nationally managed approach.

faqs.q: Does a high PSA result mean I have prostate cancer?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says a raised PSA level can be a sign of prostate cancer but can also be caused by another condition, such as an enlarged prostate, prostatitis or a urinary tract infection. It adds that around 3 in 4 men with a raised PSA level will not have cancer.

faqs.q: Does prostate cancer always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says prostate cancer often causes no symptoms at first. When symptoms appear they are usually changes to passing urine, and lower back pain and unexplained weight loss can occur in advanced cases. An enlarged prostate is a common non-cancerous cause of similar urinary symptoms.

faqs.q: Will every prostate cancer need treatment?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The NHS says treatment is not always necessary, and that prostate cancer often grows slowly and may never cause problems. Macmillan describes active surveillance as monitoring with regular PSA tests and MRI scans instead of treating straight away.

faqs.q: Who is at higher risk of prostate cancer?
faqs.a: Macmillan and Prostate Cancer UK both describe age, Black ethnicity and family history as linked with a higher risk. Macmillan says Black men have a much higher risk and tend to develop prostate cancer at a younger age. Prostate Cancer UK says changes in the BRCA genes can also raise the risk, although they are uncommon.

faqs.q: Who should I speak to if I am worried?
faqs.a: The NHS lists seeing a GP as non-urgent advice if a person has trouble passing urine or other symptoms of prostate cancer, or is worried about their risk. The NHS says a GP assesses the chance of prostate cancer using factors such as PSA levels, the prostate examination, age, family history and ethnic group, and can refer a person to hospital for further tests.

lymphoma.name: Lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin)
lymphoma.definition: Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic system, and doctors group it into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
lymphoma.overview: A painless lump or swelling in the neck, armpit or groin is the most common symptom of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, according to the NHS. Fever, night sweats, itching and unexplained weight loss are also listed. The NHS says the cause of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is not known, and a weakened immune system is among the things that can raise the risk. A biopsy of an affected lymph node is the main diagnostic test, and treatment depends on the type, how fast it grows, where it is and whether it has spread.
causes: The NHS says the cause of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is not known.
NHS 111 Wales says the exact cause of Hodgkin lymphoma is unknown.
riskFactors: A weakened immune system
Being over 50
Certain infections, such as Epstein-Barr virus or hepatitis C
Autoimmune conditions, and the immunosuppressive drugs used to treat them, which may add a slight risk
A close relative who has had non-Hodgkin lymphoma
Past exposure to Epstein-Barr virus (Hodgkin lymphoma)
signs: Painless swelling of lymph nodes in the neck, armpit or groin
complications: Possible long-term problems after treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma, including infertility and a higher risk of another cancer later
lymphoma.diagnosis: A GP asks about symptoms, may feel for lumps in the neck, armpit and groin, and refers the person to a hospital specialist for tests if non-Hodgkin lymphoma is suspected. The main test is a biopsy, in which a sample of an affected lymph node is taken and checked for signs of cancer. NHS 111 Wales says a biopsy is the only way to confirm a diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma, and that further tests then check how far it has spread. For follicular lymphoma, Lymphoma Action says diagnosis is by biopsy, followed by staging, which typically uses a CT or PET scan.
lymphoma.treatment: The NHS says treatment for non-Hodgkin lymphoma depends on how fast the lymphoma grows, where it is in the body, its type and whether it has spread. Common treatments include chemotherapy, radiotherapy and medicines that target cancer cells, including monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab. Slow-growing types may sometimes be monitored without immediate treatment, while fast-growing types need treatment straight away. For Hodgkin lymphoma, the Royal Marsden says chemotherapy and radiotherapy are the main treatments.
lymphoma.prevention: Macmillan says most people who have had infections linked to non-Hodgkin lymphoma, such as Epstein-Barr virus or Helicobacter pylori, will not develop it. For most people with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a cause is never found.
lymphoma.seekCare: Lymphoma Action says many things other than lymphoma can cause lumps, and it advises seeing a GP about a lump that lasts or keeps growing. Fever, night sweats or unexplained weight loss are also reasons to raise with a GP, who can arrange referral to a hospital specialist for tests. In an emergency, such as severe difficulty breathing, call 999; NHS 111 can advise when it is unclear how urgent a problem is.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of lymphoma?
sections.body:
The NHS describes a painless lump or swelling, usually in the neck, armpit or the top of the inner thigh (the groin), as the most common symptom of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Fever, night sweats, itching and unexplained weight loss are also listed. MedlinePlus lists swollen lymph nodes, fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss and fatigue as the usual signs of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

For Hodgkin lymphoma, MedlinePlus says the first sign is often a painless swollen lymph node with no known cause. It also lists pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs, caused by a swollen spleen or liver, among the symptoms. Lymphoma Action describes a lump or lumps in the neck, armpit or groin as the most common sign of lymphoma, and says many things that are not lymphoma can cause lumps.

sections.heading: What types of lymphoma are there, and what causes them?
sections.body:
Lymphoma is grouped into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The NHS says there are two types of Hodgkin lymphoma: classical Hodgkin lymphoma and nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma has many subtypes, and Lymphoma Action describes follicular lymphoma and MALT lymphoma among them. The NHS describes them as fast growing (high grade) or slow growing (low grade), and the type affects the treatment plan.

The NHS says the cause of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is not known, but some things can raise the risk, including a weakened immune system. Risk is higher in people over 50, and certain infections such as Epstein-Barr virus or hepatitis C, and autoimmune conditions, are also listed. Macmillan adds that a close relative with the condition is a listed factor and that most people who have had these infections will not develop lymphoma. For Hodgkin lymphoma, NHS 111 Wales says the exact cause is unknown, and it lists past exposure to Epstein-Barr virus as a risk factor.

sections.heading: How is lymphoma diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP asks about symptoms and may feel for lumps in the neck, armpit and groin. If the GP thinks non-Hodgkin lymphoma is possible, the NHS says they refer the person to a specialist at a hospital for tests. The main test is a biopsy, in which a sample of an affected lymph node is taken and checked for signs of cancer. NHS 111 Wales says a biopsy is the only way to confirm Hodgkin lymphoma, and that further tests then check how far it has spread.

For follicular lymphoma, Lymphoma Action says diagnosis is by biopsy, followed by staging, which typically uses a CT or PET scan. For MALT lymphoma, Cancer Research UK says staging usually involves a CT scan, and other staging tests can include a PET-CT scan and a bone marrow test. For MALT lymphoma that starts in the stomach, a test for Helicobacter pylori bacteria is also part of the work-up. Because treatment depends on how fast the lymphoma grows, where it is, its type and whether it has spread, the tests that establish these matter for the plan.

sections.heading: How is lymphoma treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment for non-Hodgkin lymphoma depends on how fast the lymphoma grows, where it is, its type and whether it has spread. Fast-growing types need treatment straight away, while slow-growing types may sometimes be managed by monitoring. Common treatments include chemotherapy, radiotherapy and medicines that target cancer cells, including monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab. Lymphoma Action says active monitoring, also called watch and wait, may be offered for a low-grade (slow-growing) lymphoma that is not causing problems that affect daily life. For MALT lymphoma, Lymphoma Action lists treating a linked infection, active monitoring, radiotherapy and immunochemotherapy as the main options.

For Hodgkin lymphoma, the Royal Marsden says early-stage disease may be treated with radiotherapy alone or with chemotherapy, while chemotherapy is the main treatment for more widespread disease. The NHS says targeted medicines or immunotherapy are used if Hodgkin lymphoma comes back or does not respond to treatment. NHS 111 Wales says brentuximab vedotin is available on the NHS for CD30-positive Hodgkin lymphoma in people who have already had a stem cell transplant using their own cells or cannot have chemotherapy. For slow-growing nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, the NHS says regular tests monitor the lymphoma and treatment is offered when tests show it is needed.

sections.heading: What is the outlook, and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales describes treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma as highly effective and the condition as one of the most easily treated types of cancer. The same page mentions possible long-term problems after treatment, including infertility and a higher risk of another cancer later. For non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Macmillan says high-grade lymphomas tend to respond well to treatment, while the aim for advanced low-grade disease is usually to keep it under control for as long as possible.

Lymphoma Action advises seeing a GP about a lump in the neck, armpit or groin that lasts or keeps growing, and notes that many other conditions cause lumps. The NHS also lists fever, night sweats and unexplained weight loss among the symptoms of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and a GP can arrange referral for tests.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
faqs.a: They are the two main groups of lymphoma, and the NHS has a separate page for each. Hodgkin lymphoma has two types, classical and nodular lymphocyte predominant. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma has many subtypes, and its treatment depends on how fast it grows, where it is, its type and whether it has spread. Hodgkin lymphoma is mainly treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

faqs.q: Is a lump in the neck always lymphoma?
faqs.a: No. A painless lump in the neck, armpit or groin is the most common sign of lymphoma, but many other conditions cause lumps. A GP can ask about symptoms and may feel for lumps. If lymphoma is suspected, the GP refers the person to a hospital specialist for tests.

faqs.q: Who is more likely to get non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
faqs.a: The NHS says the cause is not known, but risk is higher in people over 50 and in those with a weakened immune system. Certain infections, such as Epstein-Barr virus or hepatitis C, and autoimmune conditions are also listed. Macmillan adds that most people who have had these infections will not develop lymphoma.

faqs.q: Does everyone with lymphoma need treatment straight away?
faqs.a: Not always. The NHS says fast-growing types need treatment straight away, while slow-growing types may sometimes be managed by monitoring. Lymphoma Action describes active monitoring, also called watch and wait, for low-grade lymphoma that is not causing problems that affect daily life, with regular appointments until treatment is needed. For follicular lymphoma without troublesome symptoms, a period of active monitoring is described before any treatment.

faqs.q: What is the outlook for Hodgkin lymphoma?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales describes treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma as highly effective and the condition as one of the most easily treated types of cancer. It also mentions possible long-term problems after treatment, including infertility and a higher risk of another cancer later. A clinician can explain what the outlook means for a particular type and stage.

skin-cancer.name: Skin cancer
skin-cancer.definition: Skin cancer is a group of cancers that start in the skin, divided into melanoma and non-melanoma types.
skin-cancer.overview: Skin cancer is a group of cancers that start in the skin, divided into melanoma and non-melanoma types. In the UK, basal cell carcinoma is the most common type of non-melanoma skin cancer. Ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun or sunbeds is the most common cause. Surgery is the main treatment for non-melanoma skin cancer and for early melanoma. A mole that has changed, or a new or unusual mark or growth that does not go away, is a reason to see a GP.
causes: Ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun
Ultraviolet (UV) light from sunbeds and sunlamps
riskFactors: Pale or fair skin that burns easily in the sun
A large number of moles or freckles
A family history of skin cancer
A previous non-melanoma skin cancer
Older age
signs: A new mole, or a change in an existing mole
A mole that changes in size, shape or colour
A mole that is swollen, sore, bleeding, itchy or crusty
A growth or unusual patch on the skin that varies in colour, size and texture
A dark area under a nail that was not caused by an injury
A sore or broken (ulcerated) area, which can occur in melanoma on brown or black skin
complications: Melanoma that is very deep or has spread to the lymph nodes is more likely to return after treatment
Spread of the cancer beyond the skin, which scans or blood tests may be used to assess
skin-cancer.diagnosis: If a GP suspects melanoma, the NHS says the person should see a specialist within two weeks of seeing the GP. At the specialist appointment the mole may be removed and sent for testing (a biopsy) to check whether it is cancerous. For non-melanoma skin cancer, the specialist may recommend cutting out a small area of affected skin so that it can be checked in a laboratory for cancer, which is called an excision biopsy. If melanoma is confirmed, the NHS lists CT or MRI scans, tests of the lymph nodes and blood tests to find out whether it has spread.
skin-cancer.treatment: Surgery to remove the cancer is the main treatment for non-melanoma skin cancer, according to the NHS. Radiotherapy, medicines, photodynamic therapy and chemotherapy are also sometimes used. For melanoma, the NHS says the surgeon removes the melanoma and an area of healthy skin around it, and Cancer Research UK calls surgery the main treatment for melanoma in situ and early melanomas. Targeted medicines or immunotherapy are sometimes used for melanomas that cannot be treated with surgery.
skin-cancer.prevention: A British Association of Dermatologists leaflet says that shielding the skin from ultraviolet light lowers the number of new actinic keratoses and the risk of skin cancer. It advises clothing, a hat, UV-protective sunglasses and shade in the middle of the day, with sunscreen as extra protection rather than a replacement for them. It also advises avoiding sunlamps, sunbeds and UV tanning cabinets.
skin-cancer.seekCare: The NHS advises a non-urgent GP appointment for a mole that has changed in size, shape or colour, is painful or itchy, or is inflamed, bleeding or crusty. It also advises seeing a GP about a new or unusual mark on the skin that has not gone away after a few weeks, and about a dark area under a nail that was not caused by an injury. For non-melanoma skin cancer, the NHS advises a GP appointment for a growth that is getting bigger or has changed colour or texture, or a growth or area of skin that hurts, itches, bleeds, crusts or scabs for more than four weeks. If a GP suspects melanoma, the NHS says a specialist appointment should follow within two weeks.

sections.heading: What is skin cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS describes two broad groups, melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer, and gives each its own information. The NHS lists basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma as the two main types of non-melanoma skin cancer. In the UK, basal cell carcinoma is the most common type, with squamous cell carcinoma the second most common.

Ultraviolet (UV) light is the most common cause of both melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer, and it comes from the sun and from sunbeds. Surgery is the main treatment for non-melanoma skin cancer, and for early melanoma. For non-melanoma skin cancer, the NHS says that finding it early can mean it is easier to treat. The NHS adds that these two main types can often be treated easily. Melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer differ in how they look, so their signs are described separately below.

sections.heading: What are the signs of melanoma?
sections.body:
The NHS says a new mole, or a change in an existing mole, can be an early sign of melanoma. It describes normal moles as usually round with smooth edges and one colour, while melanomas are often an uneven shape and a mix of two or more colours. Other signs to look out for include a mole that is swollen, sore, bleeding, itchy or crusty. The NHS advises seeing a GP about a mole that has changed in size, shape or colour. It also lists a new or unusual mark on the skin that has not gone away after a few weeks, and a dark area under a nail that was not caused by an injury.

A checklist called ABCDE is often used to describe the features to look for, standing for asymmetry, border, colour, diameter and evolving. Cancer Research UK says melanoma can be harder to spot in people with brown or black skin. In these cases it may appear under a nail or on the palm of the hand or sole of the foot. It may not show the usual ABCD signs, or it may have a sore or broken (ulcerated) surface.

sections.heading: What are the signs of non-melanoma skin cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main symptom of non-melanoma skin cancer is a growth or unusual patch on the skin. These growths and patches can vary in colour, size and texture, and they appear mostly on sun-exposed areas. The NHS advises seeing a GP about a growth that is getting bigger or has changed colour or texture. It gives the same advice for a growth or area of skin that hurts, itches, bleeds, crusts or scabs for more than four weeks.

A British Association of Dermatologists leaflet says actinic keratoses, a sun-related skin change, are caused by sun exposure over many years. The leaflet lists sunbathing, sunbed use and outdoor work or leisure activities among the sources of that exposure. It advises examining the skin every few months and seeing a doctor about anything new that looks abnormal. It also advises visiting a GP if an actinic keratosis starts to become a lump or to bleed.

sections.heading: What causes skin cancer and who is at higher risk?
sections.body:
The NHS names ultraviolet (UV) light as the most common cause of melanoma and of non-melanoma skin cancer. The light comes from the sun and is also used in sunbeds. For melanoma, the NHS lists pale skin that burns easily in the sun, red or blonde hair, and blue or green eyes as risk factors. A large number of freckles or moles and a family history of skin cancer also raise the risk. Melanoma is more common in older people, though younger people can also get it.

Having brown or black skin lowers the chance of non-melanoma skin cancer, but it does not remove it. The NHS lists pale skin that burns easily, red or fair hair, using sunbeds a lot and having had a non-melanoma skin cancer before among its risk factors. Non-melanoma skin cancer is more common in older people, and people who work outdoors are at increased risk, according to Cancer Research UK. A British Association of Dermatologists leaflet says shielding the skin from UV light lowers the risk of skin cancer.

sections.heading: How is skin cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
If a GP suspects melanoma, the NHS says the person should see a specialist within two weeks of seeing the GP. At the specialist appointment the mole may be removed and sent for testing, called a biopsy, to check whether it is cancerous. The NHS says results should take about two weeks, though it may sometimes be longer. For non-melanoma skin cancer, the specialist may recommend cutting out a small area of affected skin to be checked in a laboratory. The NHS says basal cell carcinoma rarely spreads, so more tests are only needed if it is very large.

If melanoma is confirmed, the NHS lists CT or MRI scans, tests to see whether it has spread to the lymph nodes, and blood tests. Cancer Research UK adds that a PET scan can also be used. The results show how deep the cancer is and how far it has spread, which is called the stage. MedlinePlus says melanoma that is very deep, or has spread to the lymph nodes, is more likely to return after treatment.

sections.heading: How is skin cancer treated?
sections.body:
For melanoma, the NHS says the surgeon removes the melanoma and an area of healthy skin around it, and may also remove affected lymph nodes. Cancer Research UK calls surgery the main treatment for melanoma in situ and early melanomas. Targeted medicines or immunotherapy are sometimes used for melanomas that cannot be treated with surgery, and Cancer Research UK says they are the main treatments for stage 4 melanoma. The NHS says radiotherapy is sometimes used to reduce the size of large melanomas and relieve symptoms. Chemotherapy is sometimes used for advanced melanoma but does not work as well as targeted medicines and immunotherapy.

Surgery is the main treatment for non-melanoma skin cancer. Radiotherapy, medicines, photodynamic therapy and chemotherapy are also sometimes used. The treatment depends on the type of skin cancer, where it is, whether it has spread and the general health of the person. If a large area of skin is removed, skin may be taken from another part of the body to cover the area.

faqs.q: What is the difference between melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer?
faqs.a: They are two broad groups of skin cancer that the NHS describes on separate pages. The two main non-melanoma types are basal cell carcinoma, the most common in the UK, and squamous cell carcinoma. Ultraviolet light is the most common cause of both groups. Surgery is the main treatment for non-melanoma skin cancer and for early melanoma.

faqs.q: Can sunbeds cause skin cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS says ultraviolet light, which comes from the sun and is used in sunbeds, is the most common cause of melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer. It lists using sunbeds a lot as a risk factor for non-melanoma skin cancer. A British Association of Dermatologists leaflet advises avoiding sunlamps, sunbeds and UV tanning cabinets.

faqs.q: Can melanoma look different on brown or black skin?
faqs.a: Cancer Research UK says melanoma can be harder to spot in people with brown or black skin. It may appear under a nail or on the palm or sole, may not show the usual ABCD signs, or may have a sore or broken surface. The NHS advises seeing a GP about a new or unusual mark on the skin that has not gone away after a few weeks, including on the palms or soles.

faqs.q: Who is more likely to get skin cancer?
faqs.a: For melanoma, the NHS lists pale skin that burns easily, red or blonde hair, a large number of freckles or moles, and a family history of skin cancer. For non-melanoma skin cancer it also lists using sunbeds a lot and having had a non-melanoma skin cancer before. Brown or black skin lowers the chance of non-melanoma skin cancer, but does not remove it.

faqs.q: What happens if a GP thinks a mole could be melanoma?
faqs.a: The NHS says the person should see a specialist within two weeks of seeing the GP. The specialist may remove the mole and send it for testing, a biopsy, to check whether it is cancerous. If melanoma is confirmed, CT or MRI scans, lymph node tests and blood tests may follow to see whether it has spread.

faqs.q: How is non-melanoma skin cancer treated?
faqs.a: The NHS says surgery is the main treatment for non-melanoma skin cancer. Radiotherapy, medicines, photodynamic therapy and chemotherapy are also sometimes used. The choice depends on the type of skin cancer, where it is, whether it has spread and the general health of the person.

thyroid-cancer.name: Thyroid cancer
thyroid-cancer.definition: Thyroid cancer is a cancer that starts in the thyroid gland, a gland in the neck that makes hormones.
thyroid-cancer.overview: Early thyroid cancer often causes no symptoms. A common sign is a painless lump in the neck that slowly gets bigger. The main types are papillary, follicular, medullary and anaplastic cancer. Surgery is the most common treatment, and radioactive iodine is usually offered afterwards. The outlook depends on the type and stage of the cancer, and a specialist team explains it for each person.
causes: The exact cause of thyroid cancer is not known for most people
Radiotherapy to the head or neck, usually given in childhood, can increase the risk of thyroid cancer many years later
Having a close relative with thyroid cancer raises the risk, although the overall risk stays small
riskFactors: Radiotherapy to the head or neck, usually in childhood
A close relative who has had thyroid cancer
A long-standing goitre (enlarged thyroid)
Being female, as thyroid cancer is diagnosed more often in women
signs: A hard, painless lump in the front lower part of the neck that slowly gets bigger
A hoarse voice that is not getting better
Difficulty swallowing or breathing
complications: Spread to nearby lymph nodes in the neck, which may be removed during surgery
Return of the cancer after treatment, which is one reason follow-up is arranged
Low thyroid hormone levels after the thyroid is removed, which is why replacement tablets are usually needed
thyroid-cancer.diagnosis: A GP may examine the neck and arrange a blood test, and may refer the person urgently to a hospital specialist if cancer is a concern, which does not mean that cancer is certain. Blood tests mainly check thyroid function and cannot identify cancer on their own. An ultrasound scan of the neck helps estimate how likely a thyroid nodule is to be cancer and whether a biopsy is needed. A fine needle aspiration biopsy, in which a thin needle removes some cells from the lump, is the usual tissue test.
thyroid-cancer.treatment: Surgery to remove the thyroid is the most common treatment, and the surgeon may also remove nearby lymph nodes in the neck if the cancer has spread or might have spread. Radioactive iodine is usually offered after surgery to destroy any thyroid tissue left behind. After the whole thyroid is removed, hormone tablets are usually needed to replace the hormones it made. For more advanced disease, options include targeted medicines and radiotherapy.
thyroid-cancer.prevention: The causes of thyroid cancer are not known for most people, and having a risk factor does not mean that a person will develop it.
thyroid-cancer.seekCare: The NHS advises seeing a GP about a lump in the neck, a hoarse voice that is not getting better, or difficulty swallowing that is not getting better. For a person who finds it hard to breathe or has a wheezing noise when breathing, NHS advice on goitre is to call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: What is thyroid cancer and what types are there?
sections.body:
Thyroid cancer starts in the thyroid gland, which sits in the front of the neck. The main types are papillary, follicular, medullary and anaplastic cancer. Papillary is the most common type, and follicular is less common. Papillary and follicular cancers are together called differentiated thyroid cancer. The National Cancer Institute describes both as generally slow growing, although rare aggressive forms exist.

Medullary thyroid cancer is rare and starts in the C cells of the thyroid, which make a hormone called calcitonin. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is very rare and fast growing, and the National Cancer Institute calls it the most aggressive type. The type affects treatment, because radioactive iodine is used mainly for differentiated cancers and is not used for medullary thyroid cancer. Macmillan Cancer Support has separate information pages on papillary and follicular, medullary and anaplastic thyroid cancer. Care is usually planned by a multidisciplinary team, which can include specialist surgeons, oncologists, cancer nurse specialists, radiologists and histopathologists who meet to discuss the best treatment.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of thyroid cancer?
sections.body:
Early thyroid cancer often causes no symptoms, and it is sometimes found by chance on scans done for other reasons. The typical lump is in the front, lower part of the neck, and it usually feels hard, slowly gets bigger and is not painful. Other symptoms can include a hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing or breathing, and pain or pressure at the front of the neck.

Neck lumps are common and are usually caused by a less serious condition, such as an enlarged thyroid called a goitre. Thyroid cancer is uncommon, and most neck lumps turn out to be benign, which means not cancer. The NHS advises booking a GP appointment for a lump in the neck, a hoarse voice that is not getting better, or difficulty swallowing that is not getting better. If the GP is concerned about cancer, the person may be referred urgently to a hospital specialist, which does not mean that cancer is certain. NHS advice on goitre is to call 999 or go to A&E if a person finds it hard to breathe or has a wheezing noise when breathing.

sections.heading: What causes thyroid cancer and who is at risk?
sections.body:
Doctors do not know the exact cause of thyroid cancer in most people, but some risk factors can raise the chance of developing it. Having one or more risk factors does not mean that a person will get thyroid cancer. Radiotherapy to the head or neck, usually given in childhood, can increase the risk of thyroid cancer many years later, according to Cancer Research UK. A review of radiation-related thyroid cancer describes the thyroid as highly sensitive to radiation during childhood and adolescence.

Having a close relative with thyroid cancer raises the risk, and the risk is higher with more than one affected relative or a diagnosis at a young age. A long-standing goitre is listed as a risk factor, and Macmillan says some non-cancerous thyroid conditions, such as goitres and nodules, can slightly increase the risk. Macmillan also says that having an overactive or underactive thyroid does not increase the risk of thyroid cancer. Thyroid cancer is diagnosed more often in women than in men. For medullary thyroid cancer, NHS genomics education material says that genetic testing for the RET gene is offered to people diagnosed, and that relatives can be offered testing if a gene change is found.

sections.heading: How is thyroid cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP may examine the neck and arrange a blood test. Blood tests mainly check how the thyroid is working, and Macmillan notes that cancer cannot be identified from a blood test alone. The GP may refer the person to a hospital specialist for further tests.

An ultrasound scan of the neck is usually the first imaging test once a lump or nodule has been found. Features seen on ultrasound, such as the size and edges of the nodule, help estimate how likely it is to be cancer and whether a biopsy is needed. Fine needle aspiration is the usual tissue test and is often guided by ultrasound. In this test a thin needle removes some cells from the lump so that they can be examined under a microscope. If the result is unclear, a core needle biopsy or a surgical biopsy may follow. The National Cancer Institute describes thyroglobulin and calcitonin blood tests as supporting markers, and advises that biopsy samples can be reviewed by a pathologist with experience of thyroid cancer.

sections.heading: How is thyroid cancer treated?
sections.body:
Surgery is the most common treatment for thyroid cancer, according to the NHS. The operation removes the thyroid, which is called a thyroidectomy, and the surgeon may also remove some lymph nodes in the neck if the cancer has spread or might have spread to them. Radioactive iodine is usually offered after surgery, and its purpose is to destroy any thyroid tissue left over. It is usually given as a capsule or tablet, and treatment can involve a short stay in hospital.

The thyroid and most differentiated thyroid cancer cells take up iodine, so the radiation acts on them directly. Radioactive iodine is not used to treat medullary thyroid cancer. After the whole thyroid is removed, hormone tablets are usually needed to replace the hormones it made, and some hospitals note that the tablets can also help stop the cancer coming back. For more advanced disease, the National Cancer Institute lists targeted therapy and external radiotherapy as options, and chemotherapy is often combined with radiotherapy in anaplastic thyroid cancer. The multidisciplinary team discusses the best treatment, including the extent of surgery, and then talks it through with the patient.

sections.heading: What happens after treatment and what is the outlook?
sections.body:
After treatment, follow-up checks look for any remaining or returning cancer. Neck ultrasound and blood tests, including thyroglobulin, are the main follow-up tools in differentiated thyroid cancer. Macmillan explains that thyroglobulin is normally absent once the thyroid is removed and radioactive iodine given, so a detectable level can suggest remaining cancer cells. For medullary thyroid cancer, Cancer Research UK lists calcitonin as the tumour marker, and levels can rise for reasons other than cancer.

How often follow-up is needed varies with the risk of the cancer coming back, and one patient guide says that people with low-risk cancers removed by surgery may not need follow-up care. Replacement hormone tablets, usually levothyroxine, are typically needed for life after the thyroid is removed. The outlook depends on the type and stage of the thyroid cancer, and the specialist team can explain what this means for each person.

faqs.q: Is every lump in the neck thyroid cancer?
faqs.a: No. Neck lumps are common and are usually caused by a less serious condition, such as an enlarged thyroid, and thyroid cancer is uncommon. A new lump should still be checked, and the NHS advises booking a GP appointment. The GP may examine the neck, arrange a blood test and refer the person to a specialist if cancer is a concern.

faqs.q: Does thyroid cancer always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. Early thyroid cancer often causes no symptoms and is sometimes found by chance on scans done for other reasons. When symptoms do appear, a painless lump in the neck that slowly gets bigger is typical. Others include a hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing or breathing.

faqs.q: Will someone need thyroid hormone tablets after treatment?
faqs.a: After the whole thyroid is removed, hormone tablets are usually needed to replace the hormones it made. The British Thyroid Foundation names levothyroxine as the replacement hormone, and it is typically taken for life. Some hospitals note that the tablets can also help stop the cancer coming back. Blood tests and scans after treatment check for any remaining cancer.

faqs.q: What is the outlook for thyroid cancer?
faqs.a: The outlook depends on the type of thyroid cancer and its stage. Papillary and follicular cancers are generally slow growing, whereas anaplastic thyroid cancer is very rare, fast growing and the most aggressive type. Macmillan has separate information on each type, and a specialist team can explain the outlook for each person.

bladder-cancer.name: Bladder cancer
bladder-cancer.definition: Bladder cancer is cancer that forms in the tissues of the bladder, the organ that stores urine.
bladder-cancer.overview: Blood in the urine is the most common sign of bladder cancer, according to Macmillan and MedlinePlus. Many people with blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer, but the NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111. Smoking is the biggest known risk factor for bladder cancer. Treatment depends on the stage and type of the cancer, and the NHS says surgery is usually offered first, with chemotherapy, radiotherapy or immunotherapy added in some cases.
causes: Smoking is the biggest known risk factor, and estimates of its share of cases vary between sources
Contact with certain chemicals at work, such as aromatic amines used in some industries, is also linked to the cancer
Repeated urinary infections and long-term bladder stones have been linked to a less common squamous cell type
riskFactors: Smoking, including heavy and long-term smoking
Exposure to certain chemicals in the workplace
Being male
Being older
Repeated urinary infections or long-term bladder stones, linked to a less common squamous cell type
signs: Visible blood in the urine, which may look pink, red or dark brown
Blood that is only found on a urine test
Burning when passing urine, passing urine more often or feeling the bladder has not emptied
complications: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer often comes back after treatment
Some tumours can progress, so follow-up after treatment is usually long-term
Treatment placed into the bladder, such as BCG, can cause bladder irritation, blood in the urine and fever
bladder-cancer.diagnosis: A GP usually sees a person first and may ask for a urine sample to be sent for testing. The sample is checked for infection and, in some cases, for cancer cells. If the GP thinks cancer is possible or is unsure of the cause, they refer the person to a urologist, a specialist in the urinary tract. The main test is a cystoscopy, in which a thin camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder. Imaging such as a CT urogram may also be used, and abnormal areas can be removed in an operation called TURBT so they can be tested for cancer.
bladder-cancer.treatment: Treatment depends on the stage and type of the cancer. The NHS says surgery is usually offered first, and chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy may be added depending on the case. For early-stage disease, treatments such as BCG or mitomycin can be placed directly into the bladder. Removing the whole bladder, called cystectomy, is used for higher-risk or muscle-invasive disease, and radiotherapy with chemotherapy is another approach.
bladder-cancer.prevention: Smoking is the biggest known risk factor, and workplace exposure to certain chemicals is also linked to the cancer.
bladder-cancer.seekCare: The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment, or contacting NHS 111, for blood in the urine, even if it is a small amount or there are no other symptoms. NHS 111 Wales says blood in the urine should be checked even if it comes and goes. Many people with blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer, as infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate are other possible causes, but it still needs checking.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of bladder cancer?
sections.body: Blood in the urine is the most common sign of bladder cancer, according to Macmillan and MedlinePlus. The blood can be visible, or present in amounts too small to see and found only on a urine test. The NHS says blood in the urine may look pink, red or dark brown. Macmillan says it can start suddenly and may come and go. Other symptoms include a burning feeling when passing urine, needing to pass urine more often, rushing to the toilet, difficulty passing urine and a feeling that the bladder has not fully emptied. Pain in the lower tummy or back is less common. Macmillan says these urinary symptoms are usually caused by an infection, an overactive bladder or an enlarged prostate rather than cancer. Many people with blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer. The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment, or contacting NHS 111, for blood in the urine, even if it is a small amount or there are no other symptoms. NHS 111 Wales says blood in the urine should be checked even if it comes and goes.

sections.heading: What causes bladder cancer, and who is at higher risk?
sections.body: Smoking is the biggest known risk factor for bladder cancer. A Bristol NHS urology page explains that chemicals from tobacco are filtered into the urine and sit against the bladder lining. Estimates of how much smoking contributes vary: NHS 111 Wales says more than a third of cases are caused by it, while Macmillan suggests about half. The Royal Marsden says heavy, long-term smoking carries the most risk. Exposure to certain chemicals at work is another recognised factor. These include aromatic amines and aniline dyes, with jobs in dye production, textiles, rubber, plastics and paint linked to higher risk. Cancers linked to these chemicals can take many years to appear, so past exposure still matters. NHS pages list being older and being male as other factors. Repeated urinary infections and long-term or untreated bladder stones have been linked to a less common type called squamous cell bladder cancer. Having a risk factor does not mean a person will develop bladder cancer.

sections.heading: How is bladder cancer diagnosed?
sections.body: A GP usually sees a person first and may ask for a urine sample to be sent for testing. The sample is checked for infection and, in some cases, for cancer cells. The GP may also arrange blood tests. If the GP thinks cancer is possible or is unsure of the cause, they refer the person to a urologist, a specialist in the urinary tract. The main test is a cystoscopy, in which a thin camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder. It can be done while awake with a local anaesthetic, or under general anaesthetic. A small sample of the bladder lining, called a biopsy, may be taken for testing. If cystoscopy shows abnormal areas, an operation called TURBT can remove them so that the tissue can be tested for cancer. Imaging such as an ultrasound scan, a CT urogram or an MRI scan may also be used.

sections.heading: How is bladder cancer treated?
sections.body: Treatment depends on the stage and type of the cancer. The NHS says surgery is usually offered first, and chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy may be added depending on the case. For non-muscle-invasive disease, an operation called TURBT removes visible tumours through the urethra. For early disease, a single dose of chemotherapy can be placed directly into the bladder through a catheter after surgery. Treatments such as BCG immunotherapy or mitomycin chemotherapy can also be placed directly into the bladder for non-muscle-invasive disease. A review describes BCG as the standard treatment after surgery for high-risk non-muscle-invasive disease. Removing the whole bladder, called cystectomy, is used for higher-risk or muscle-invasive disease and is major surgery. Radiotherapy may be used instead of surgery, and is often combined with chemotherapy, which is called chemoradiotherapy. Reviews describe radical cystectomy as the standard option for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, with chemoradiotherapy as a bladder-sparing alternative for some people. One review notes that no randomised trials have directly compared the two approaches.

sections.heading: Can bladder cancer come back, and what is living with it like?
sections.body: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer often comes back after treatment. Reviews describe high rates of recurrence in the first years after treatment, and some tumours can progress. For this reason, follow-up is long-term, and one review describes it as lifelong. Cystoscopy is the standard method of follow-up, often combined with urine tests and imaging of the upper urinary tract. The schedule is usually adapted to the risk category of the tumour. Urine-based tests are being studied, but reviews say none has yet replaced cystoscopy in routine practice. Treatment placed into the bladder can have side effects. A systematic review linked BCG to bladder irritation, blood in the urine and fever in a substantial share of people. A quality-of-life review found that treatment-related side effects were the main reason people stopped treatment. One comparison reported more systemic side effects with BCG than with mitomycin C. After bladder-sparing chemoradiotherapy, reviews say lifelong surveillance is needed because the risk of recurrence remains for years.

faqs.q: Is blood in the urine always bladder cancer?
faqs.a: No. Many people with blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer. Infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate are other possible causes of blood in the urine. The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment, or contacting NHS 111, for blood in the urine, even if it is a small amount or there are no other symptoms. NHS 111 Wales says blood in the urine should be checked even if it comes and goes.

faqs.q: What is a cystoscopy?
faqs.a: A cystoscopy is the main test for bladder cancer. A thin camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder. It can be done while awake with a local anaesthetic, or under general anaesthetic. A small sample of the bladder lining, called a biopsy, may be taken for testing.

faqs.q: Does smoking cause bladder cancer?
faqs.a: Smoking is the biggest known risk factor for bladder cancer. Estimates of how much smoking contributes vary: NHS 111 Wales says more than a third of cases are caused by it, while Macmillan suggests about half. Chemicals from tobacco are filtered into the urine and sit against the bladder lining. Some chemicals used in workplaces are also linked.

faqs.q: What treatments are used for bladder cancer?
faqs.a: Treatment depends on the stage and type of the cancer. The NHS says surgery is usually offered first, and chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy may be added depending on the case. For non-muscle-invasive disease, an operation called TURBT removes visible tumours through the urethra. Radiotherapy may be used instead of surgery, and is often combined with chemotherapy, which is called chemoradiotherapy.

faqs.q: Can bladder cancer come back?
faqs.a: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer often comes back after treatment. Reviews describe high rates of recurrence in the first years after treatment, and some tumours can progress. For this reason, follow-up is long-term, and one review describes it as lifelong. Cystoscopy is the standard method of follow-up, often combined with urine tests and imaging of the upper urinary tract.

testicular-cancer.name: Testicular cancer
aliases: germ cell tumour of the testis
testicular-cancer.definition: Testicular cancer is a cancer that starts in a testicle, one of the two glands in the scrotum.
testicular-cancer.overview: Some people with testicular cancer have no symptoms, and the most common sign is a lump or swelling in a testicle. It can affect anyone who has testicles, including trans women, and Macmillan says it is most likely between the ages of 25 and 40. Most lumps in the scrotum are not cancer, and testicular cancer is rare. MedlinePlus calls it one of the most treatable and curable cancers, and removing the affected testicle is the main treatment, according to the NHS.
causes: The exact cause of testicular cancer is not known, according to MedlinePlus and Macmillan
Most testicular cancers are germ cell tumours of two main types, seminoma and non-seminoma
riskFactors: An undescended testicle
A family history of testicular cancer
A previous testicular cancer
Male infertility
Ethnicity, as it is more common in white men
signs: A lump or swelling in a testicle, or a testicle that has become larger
A scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard
Tender or swollen breasts, occasionally
complications: Spread to other parts of the body, such as the lungs, abdomen, pelvis, back or brain
Effects on fertility from chemotherapy or radiotherapy
Lower testosterone levels in some people after treatment
testicular-cancer.diagnosis: A GP examines the testicles. If cancer is possible, an urgent referral to hospital may follow, and having symptoms does not definitely mean cancer. An ultrasound scan of the scrotum is the usual first test, and blood tests for substances called tumour markers are also used. The diagnosis is usually confirmed by removing the affected testicle and having a pathologist examine the tissue.
testicular-cancer.treatment: Macmillan and Cancer Research UK describe treatment as surgery, chemotherapy and in some cases radiotherapy, depending on the type of tumour and whether it has spread. The NHS says the main treatment is surgery to remove the testicle, called orchidectomy. Because some treatments can affect fertility, the NHS says people are offered the chance to store sperm, known as sperm banking, before treatment starts.
testicular-cancer.prevention: MedlinePlus says the exact cause of testicular cancer is poorly understood. Several NHS trusts suggest checking the testicles about once a month so that a change is noticed, though MedlinePlus says experts do not know whether self-exams lower the chance of dying from testicular cancer in people without symptoms or risk factors.
testicular-cancer.seekCare: The NHS advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in one or both testicles, or a testicle that is getting bigger. A GP appointment is the usual route, and the GP can arrange an urgent hospital referral if cancer is possible. Most lumps turn out to have other causes, but any new lump, swelling or unusual pain is worth having assessed.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of testicular cancer?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says some people with testicular cancer have no symptoms, and that some cases do not cause symptoms until the cancer is advanced. The NHS lists a lump or swelling in a testicle, a testicle getting bigger, an ache or pain in a testicle or the scrotum, and a scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard. Cancer Research UK says a lump can be about the size of a pea or larger.

Less common symptoms listed by the NHS include an ache in the back or lower tummy, losing weight without trying, a cough, difficulty breathing or swallowing, and a sore or swollen chest. MedlinePlus adds that enlarged breast tissue can be a sign, although it can occur normally in teenage boys. When the cancer has spread, MedlinePlus says symptoms can appear in the lungs, abdomen, pelvis, back or brain.

Lumps in the scrotum have many different causes, and testicular cancer is a rare cause. Having these symptoms does not definitely mean a person has testicular cancer, the NHS says, but it is important to have them checked by a GP.

sections.heading: What causes testicular cancer and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus and Macmillan say the exact cause of testicular cancer is not known. Macmillan lists an undescended testicle and a family history of the disease among the things that may raise the risk. Macmillan also lists ethnicity, and a published review links male infertility with a higher risk of testicular cancer. Having a risk factor does not mean a person will develop the disease, and lacking one does not rule it out, Macmillan says.

The NHS says testicular cancer is most common in men aged 15 to 49, while Macmillan says it is most likely between the ages of 25 and 40. Macmillan and an NHS trust say non-seminomas most often affect people aged 15 to 35. Orchid and Cambridge University Hospitals describe seminomas as affecting people from about 25 to 55, though sources vary on the exact range.

The two main types, seminoma and non-seminoma, are both germ cell tumours, and a mix of the two can occur.

sections.heading: Checking the testicles and seeing a GP
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in one or both testicles, or if a testicle is getting bigger. Several NHS bodies, such as the Christie NHS Foundation Trust, suggest getting to know how the testicles normally feel, with a check about once a month, so that a new lump is noticed. The Christie says a normal testicle feels smooth and firm, and that it is normal for one testicle to be slightly larger or to hang lower. The epididymis, a soft coiled tube at the back of each testicle, is not a problem, and harmless cysts can form there.

Macmillan says it is still important to have any change checked. Macmillan notes that a trans woman who has testicles may feel uncomfortable or upset about checking this part of the body, but that changes should still be checked.

The GP examines the testicles. If cancer is possible, an urgent referral to hospital may follow, and the NHS stresses that symptoms do not definitely mean cancer.

sections.heading: How is testicular cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
The National Cancer Institute lists a testicular ultrasound, which uses sound waves to look at the testicles, as the first test. Blood tests for substances called tumour markers, such as AFP and beta-hCG, are also used. An NHS England guideline says blood for these markers is best taken before surgery when an ultrasound shows a cancer.

The diagnosis is confirmed by removing the testicle through a cut in the groin, and a pathologist then examines the tissue to identify the type of tumour. The two main types of testicular cancer, seminoma and non-seminoma, are treated differently, so identifying the type is part of the diagnosis. The treatment plan also depends on whether the cancer has spread.

After diagnosis, CT scans of the chest, abdomen and pelvis are commonly used to stage the cancer, together with the blood tumour markers.

sections.heading: How is testicular cancer treated?
sections.body:
Macmillan and Cancer Research UK describe treatment as surgery, chemotherapy and in some cases radiotherapy, depending on the type of tumour and whether it has spread. The NHS says the main treatment is surgery to remove the testicle, called orchidectomy. Cancer Research UK says having one testicle removed does not usually affect the ability to have children, although the remaining testicle sometimes does not work as well, which could reduce fertility.

MedlinePlus says chemotherapy has greatly improved survival for people with both seminomas and non-seminomas. For an early seminoma, options after surgery include surveillance, a single course of the chemotherapy drug carboplatin, or radiotherapy, although radiotherapy is now mainly kept for people who cannot have chemotherapy. For an early non-seminoma, surveillance, meaning regular check-ups and tests, is an option when the risk of the cancer returning is low, and the alternative is usually a short course of chemotherapy.

Which option is suggested depends on the type of tumour, the stage and the chance of the cancer coming back.

sections.heading: Fertility, follow-up and living with testicular cancer
sections.body:
Chemotherapy and radiotherapy may affect sperm production, and Cancer Research UK says fertility can often return after treatment, though this may take time. In some cases sperm production does not fully recover, although the National Cancer Institute says most men can father children after treatment. Orchid says sperm banking may be advised before an orchidectomy if chemotherapy is likely to be needed or the other testicle may produce little sperm. Macmillan says that a person who has not stored sperm can still do so after surgery if further treatment is offered. Orchid notes that banking has limits, as a low sperm count, poor sperm quality and the freezing and thawing process can all affect the sperm, and that stored sperm is held for 10 years at first, with the period able to be extended. Orchid and Macmillan both provide information on fertility and sex after testicular cancer.

Studies report that testosterone levels can fall after treatment in some people, and reviews recommend checking testosterone levels during follow-up. Testicular cancer is generally described as highly treatable, and MedlinePlus calls it one of the most treatable and curable cancers.

faqs.q: Is a lump in a testicle always cancer?
faqs.a: No. Lumps in the scrotum have many different causes, and testicular cancer is a rare one. The NHS still advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in one or both testicles, or a testicle that is getting bigger. Having these symptoms does not definitely mean cancer, but they are worth having checked.

faqs.q: Can testicular cancer be cured?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus describes testicular cancer as one of the most treatable and curable cancers. The NHS says treatment depends on the type of tumour and whether it has spread, and MedlinePlus says chemotherapy has greatly improved survival. The outlook for any one person depends on the type and stage of the cancer.

faqs.q: Does removing a testicle affect fertility?
faqs.a: Cancer Research UK says having one testicle removed does not usually affect the ability to have children, although the remaining testicle sometimes does not work as well. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy can affect sperm production, so the NHS says people are offered sperm banking before treatment starts. Orchid has a page on fertility and testicular cancer.

faqs.q: Who can get testicular cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS and Macmillan say testicular cancer can affect anyone who has testicles. Macmillan lists men, trans women and people assigned male at birth among them. Macmillan notes that checking this part of the body may feel uncomfortable or upsetting for a trans woman, and that changes should still be checked.

faqs.q: Does testicular cancer always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. MedlinePlus says some people have no symptoms, and some cases do not cause symptoms until the cancer is advanced. When symptoms do appear, the NHS lists a lump or swelling, a larger testicle, an ache or pain, and a heavy, firm or hard scrotum.
